FREE GUIDE / BUSINESS

START WITH WHAT MUST CONTINUE

A small-business continuity plan is stronger when it identifies critical services, dependencies, workable fallbacks and who owns the decisions.

Define the critical functions

  1. List the few activities that must continue for the business to operate safely and serve customers.
  2. For each activity, decide the maximum tolerable downtime and who owns the decision.
  3. Map the dependencies: people, premises, power, internet, suppliers, data and equipment.
  4. Write one realistic manual or alternative process for each critical function.
  5. Keep essential contacts available offline and agree who communicates with staff, customers and suppliers.

Plan for loss, not one disaster

Continuity planning is stronger when it asks what happens if a critical resource becomes unavailable, rather than trying to predict every possible cause.

Test the plan

Run a short tabletop exercise: assume one critical dependency has failed. Record what becomes unclear, then fix those gaps before a real incident. Current NCSC guidance similarly emphasises understanding critical services, dependencies, feasible workarounds and exercising plans.

Keep it operational.
A continuity document is useful only if the people who need it can find it, understand it and use the fallback when normal systems are unavailable.
